title: Trump Refers Habba's Claim of a Missing Kennedy Center Donation Under Grenell to White House Counsel
institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts; White House Counsel's Office
status: Under White House counsel and Kennedy Center review; allegation unproven and denied
what_changed:
Alina Habba, President Trump's former personal attorney, told Trump in the Oval Office that Ric Grenell, who ran the Kennedy Center from February 2025 until March 2026, **failed to deposit a multimillion-dollar donation to the center that, she said, Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon, who later became her husband, arranged in May 2025.** Axios, citing four senior administration officials and three other people briefed on the dispute, reported on Oct. 14, 2026 that Trump referred the allegation to White House Counsel Will Scharf to look into. According to Habba's account, Grenell persuaded Mildon in the spring of 2025 to fold the donation into a $17.6 million wire transfer for a business deal involving a U.S. company. Habba first put the donation at $17 million, then at $5.6 million; Axios's sources also described it as nearly $6 million. Grenell called the claim "absurd" and a lie, saying "I've never received any payment from him at all." A senior administration official said the claims were only allegations. When Axios reported, counsel had asked for documentation but received none; the New York Times later reported that Mildon's lawyer sent Scharf text messages and a wire transfer receipt that night. Grenell denies sending a text attributed to him, and no outlet has verified the documents. Kennedy Center staff who searched for the donation in late 2025 could not find it; the only record they found showed Mildon owed a $270,000 pledge, which he paid on Oct. 13, 2026, after the New York Times asked about it. The center says it is reviewing relevant pledges and funds. The dispute reportedly grew out of Grenell and Mildon's shared interests in Venezuela.

Update 2026-10-21: Axios reported on Oct. 19, 2026 that the White House counsel is investigating a May 3, 2025 text, supplied by Mildon's attorneys and denied by Grenell, that reads: "Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you'll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS." Mildon alleges that at Grenell's direction he wired $17.6 million to Texas Armament & Technology (TXAT), a Houston-based defense company, to be split between a Congo deal and nearly $6 million for the Kennedy Center; sources told Axios the White House also received a May 29, 2025 financial record showing the transfer. Contrary to what Habba first told Trump, the money did not appear to come from Mildon's own account: a White House official told Axios it was wired from Congo's "Ministère des Finances" in Kinshasa, and the New York Times reported it came from a bank account affiliated with the Congolese government. Mildon has told the Times he serves as an adviser to the Congolese president and holds a Congolese diplomatic passport. Grenell acknowledged consulting for TXAT in 2024 but says he had no connection to it when the transfer was made and denies any connection to the transfer. Habba and Mildon married in September 2026; Will Scharf, the White House counsel leading the inquiry, attended the wedding, the Times reported.

estimated_impact.caveat: Every dollar figure here comes from Habba's side or from anonymous officials; no audit, filing or official finding confirms any money went missing, and the center's own search found only a $270,000 pledge.

confidence_note: LOW confidence on the underlying allegation, HIGH confidence that it was made and referred. Axios broke the story from four senior administration officials and three other insiders, and the New York Times and Washington Post confirmed the Oval Office account independently, with Grenell's on-record denial. The New York Times reported that Mildon's lawyer sent Scharf text messages and a wire transfer receipt on Oct. 14; Grenell disputes at least one of the texts, and no outlet has verified the documents. Frame it as an unproven accusation under internal review, not as a finding of missing money. Update 2026-10-21: Axios reviewed the May 2025 text Grenell denies sending, and a source said Scharf plans to verify its digital footprint. A White House official says the $17.6 million came from Congo's Finance Ministry rather than Mildon, contradicting Habba's first account; the Times reported that Scharf, who leads the inquiry, attended the Mildons' wedding.

title: Trump Orders Every Agency to Stop Funding NPR and PBS; Judge Strikes It Down as Viewpoint Discrimination
institution: National Public Radio (NPR) and the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS); federal grant-making agencies including the NEA, the Education Department and FEMA
status: Ruled unconstitutional: on Mar. 31, 2026 a federal judge permanently barred six agencies from carrying out the order's directive to end all NPR and PBS funding. The government did not appeal, and the remaining claims were dismissed in July 2026. Congress's separate cut to CPB stands.
what_changed: On May 1, 2025, three days after he moved to fire three members of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB) board, President Trump signed Executive Order 14290, "Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media" (90 Fed. Reg. 19415). Its purpose section said Americans "have the right to expect that if their tax dollars fund public broadcasting at all, they fund only fair, accurate, unbiased, and nonpartisan news coverage," and that neither NPR nor PBS "presents a fair, accurate, or unbiased portrayal of current events to taxpaying citizens." It told the CPB board to cancel direct funding of NPR and PBS and to bar local stations from using federal money for their programming (Section 2); told the heads of all agencies to "identify and terminate, to the maximum extent consistent with applicable law, any direct or indirect funding of NPR and PBS" (Section 3(a)); told agencies to review any remaining grants and contracts with the two for compliance (Section 3(b)); and told the Secretary of Health and Human Services to check whether they were complying with a statutory ban on employment discrimination (Section 3(c)). Agencies moved quickly, according to the court's later findings. On May 2, 2025, the National Endowment for the Arts terminated two NPR grants, one for literary content and one for music programming, saying the projects no longer carried out agency priorities as determined by the President. The same day, the Education Department terminated the "Ready to Learn" grant, which had awarded $78 million jointly to CPB and PBS for children's educational programming, calling it an inappropriate use of federal funds; the shortfall **resulted in the termination of 22 employees on the PBS KIDS team**. Later in May, FEMA paused its Next Generation Warning System grant program, much of which flows to PBS member stations, for about three weeks, and on July 15, 2025 the NEA denied NPR's application for an arts-projects grant without explanation. NPR and three Colorado stations (Aspen Public Radio, Colorado Public Radio and KSUT Public Radio) sued on May 27, 2025 (No. 1:25-cv-01674), and PBS and Minnesota's Lakeland PBS sued on May 30 (No. 1:25-cv-01722); both cases went to U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss in Washington, D.C., who consolidated them in February 2026. The government argued that the claims were not ripe because no particular funding decision was before the court, that it may choose which speech to subsidize, and that the President is not subject to the Administrative Procedure Act. While the cases were pending, Congress rescinded CPB's funding and CPB dissolved. On March 31, 2026, Moss declared Sections 1 and 3(a) of the order "unlawful and unenforceable because they are viewpoint discriminatory and retaliatory in violation of the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause," and permanently barred the Office of Management and Budget, the Treasury, the NEA, the Education Department, the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA from implementing or enforcing them. "The message is clear: NPR and PBS need not apply for any federal benefit because the President disapproves of their 'left-wing' coverage of the news," he wrote. He found the claims about CPB moot because "CPB no longer exists," left the Section 3(b) and 3(c) claims open, and said his order does not apply to the President himself. A White House spokeswoman, Abigail Jackson, called it "a ridiculous ruling by an activist judge," said "NPR and PBS have no right to receive taxpayer funds," and said the administration "looks forward to ultimate victory on the issue." At the parties' joint request, the court entered partial final judgment on April 23, 2026, and the government did not appeal from it. On July 16, 2026, the broadcasters and the government agreed to dismiss the remaining Section 3(b) and 3(c) claims without prejudice, and the court closed the case the next day. The ruling did not restore the money Congress rescinded from CPB.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed Executive Order 14290. The White House fact sheet issued with it said "NPR and PBS have fueled partisanship and left-wing propaganda with taxpayer dollars, which is highly inappropriate and an improper use of taxpayers' money, as President Trump has stated." Days earlier he had posted: "REPUBLICANS MUST DEFUND AND TOTALLY DISASSOCIATE THEMSELVES FROM NPR & PBS, THE RADICAL LEFT 'MONSTERS' THAT SO BADLY HURT OUR COUNTRY!"

estimated_impact.summary: The order cut NPR and PBS off from every federal program on the basis of their news coverage, not the merits of any application, and agencies acted in line with it within a day: two NEA grants to NPR and a $78 million children's-programming grant to CPB and PBS were terminated, the latter costing 22 PBS KIDS jobs, and FEMA briefly paused an emergency-alert grant program that funds PBS stations. The court ended the order's core directive about 11 months later. Federal grants outside CPB were 6% of PBS's 2025 budget, and NPR had received NEA grants every year for 27 years.

estimated_impact.caveat: The figures come from the court's opinion, which drew on the broadcasters' sworn declarations and the government's own filings. No source found here says whether the terminated NEA and Ready to Learn grants were later restored after the injunction; NPR said the ruling "does not restore lost federal funding." The far larger loss to public media came from Congress's rescission of CPB's funding, which this order did not cause and the ruling did not touch.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence. The order's text is in the Federal Register, and the court history rests on the court's own filings: the March 31, 2026 opinion and order, the April 23 partial final judgment, and the July 16 joint stipulation, which states that the government "did not appeal from that partial final judgment." The Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case summary and the ACLU of D.C. case page ("The government did not appeal") agree. The administration's case is put fairly by its own words: the order said no outlet has a constitutional right to taxpayer subsidies and that the government may decide which activities to subsidize, citing the public broadcasting law's bar on CPB supporting any political party, and in court the government argued it may choose which speech to fund. The judge accepted that the government may fund its own speech and pick grantees on legitimate criteria, but held that it may not use the power of the purse to punish disfavored expression. Frame it as a court ruling, now final, that the order's core was unconstitutional; Sections 3(b) and 3(c) were never ruled on.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The order was one of several 2025 moves against public broadcasting, alongside the attempted firing of CPB board members and the rescission of CPB's funding. See also: Congress Rescinded $1.1B From Public Broadcasting; CPB Dissolved After 58 Years.
